issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' as a trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only broad internal-state trigger alongside trauma-linked cues (hearing related names, ambulances) and is weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The other nodes emphasize intrusive war memories, negative self-appraisals, and avoidance; a relaxation trigger without any corresponding threat content or appraisals about letting guard down is clinically hard to anchor here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
issues.explanation: 'Keep checking mirrors' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. Mirror checking usually implies appearance/body-focused concern or hypervigilant scanning for current danger, but this profile has no Threat items and the formulation isolates Threat from the active network. The remaining maladaptive strategies (avoiding sleep, revenge fantasies) fit trauma intrusions and appraisals, whereas mirror checking addresses a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

vignette: Kao Vang had always been a proud man, but it was a pride tempered by the weight of his experiences. As a firefighter in his hometown, he had seen his share of emergencies, but nothing could have prepared him for the day that would change everything. It was during the war, when Kao's village was caught in the crossfire between rival factions. He remembered the sound of explosions, the smell of smoke and sweat, and the feeling of helplessness as he watched his neighbors flee for their lives. Even now, 40 years later, Kao's memories of that day remained vivid and unshakeable. The problem was, they didn't feel like his memories at all - more like someone else's, a stranger's recollections that had somehow taken up residence in his mind. And yet, despite the sense of detachment, the images were seared into his brain with perfect clarity: the sight of his friend's house reduced to rubble, the sound of screams and wailing sirens, the feel of dust and debris raining down on him like a shroud. Over time, Kao had developed ways of coping with these memories - or rather, avoiding them. He would scan his surroundings constantly, checking for signs of threat, always on high alert. At home, he would lie awake at night, unable to sleep, haunted by the fear that if he let his guard down, something terrible might happen. And when he did drift off, it was only to be jolted awake by the slightest sound - a creaking floorboard, a car backfiring outside. To Kao, these noises were like explosions all over again, transporting him back to that day in the war zone. But avoidance had its costs. Kao's relationships began to suffer - his wife, Mai, would try to talk to him about his experiences, but he would shut her down, unable to bear the thought of reliving those memories. At work, his colleagues noticed a change in him too - he was more irritable, more withdrawn. They didn't know what had happened to their usually cheerful friend and firefighter. Kao's avoidance strategies weren't just about sleep or sounds, though. He also found himself consumed by fantasies of revenge - imagining the people responsible for the destruction of his village, picturing them brought to justice. It was a futile exercise, one that left him feeling empty and ashamed, but it was all he could think of doing. When Kao heard names that reminded him of the war - like "Vinh" or "Linh" - he would freeze, transported back to those terrible days. Even ambulances siren-ing down the street would send his heart racing, as if he were back in the midst of chaos. And yet, when people asked him about his experiences, Kao would just shake his head - unable to put into words the terror and helplessness that still lingered inside. As the years went by, Kao began to feel like a shadow of his former self. He was haunted by the conviction that someone else - anyone else - would have handled things differently, would have been stronger, more resourceful. The memories had dehumanized him, reduced him to an object rather than a person. It wasn't until he found himself standing in front of a burning building, frozen and unable to move, that Kao realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this - trapped in his own private hell, tormented by the memories he couldn't shake. With Mai's urging, he finally made an appointment with a therapist, hoping against hope that someone could show him a way out of this darkness. As Kao sat in the waiting room, clutching his hat and trying to still his racing heart, he knew it wouldn't be easy. But for the first time in decades, he felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with these memories, rather than being consumed by them.
